lessons.title: Factorial and Counting Principle
lessons.concept: Counting problems often use the multiplication principle: if one task can be done in m ways and another in n ways, together they can be done in m*n ways (when choices are independent in sequence). Factorial n! = n*(n-1)*...*1 counts arrangements of n distinct objects in a row, with 0! defined as 1.
lessons.formula: n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 1, 0! = 1; sequential choices: total ways = product of ways at each step
lessons.worked_example: Arrange 4 distinct books on a shelf: 4! = 24 ways. If you choose a shirt (3 options) and pants (2 options), outfits = 3 x 2 = 6.
mistakes: Adding instead of multiplying when choices happen in sequence
Miscounting when constraints reduce options at later steps

lessons.title: Permutations (Arrangements)
lessons.concept: A permutation is an arrangement where order matters. The number of permutations of n distinct objects taken r at a time is the number of ordered selections of r from n.
lessons.formula: P(n,r) = n! / (n-r)! for 0 <= r <= n. Special case: arranging all n distinct objects gives n!.
lessons.worked_example: How many 3-letter arrangements from letters A,B,C,D with no repetition? P(4,3)=4!/(1!)=24. First position 4 choices, second 3, third 2: 4x3x2=24.
mistakes: Using permutations when order does not matter (should use combinations)
Forgetting to reduce available choices when repetition is not allowed

lessons.title: Combinations (Selections)
lessons.concept: A combination is a selection where order does not matter. Choosing r objects from n is the same group regardless of arrangement, so combinations count fewer outcomes than permutations for r >= 2.
lessons.worked_example: Select 2 students from 5 for a team: C(5,2)=5!/(2!3!)=10. The pair (A,B) is the same team as (B,A), so order is ignored.
mistakes: Treating selections as ordered when the problem states committee/team/group
Using C(n,r) when positions/roles make order important

questions.question: From 5 men and 4 women, a team of 3 people is to be formed with exactly 2 men and 1 woman. How many such teams are possible?
questions.explanation: Choose 2 men from 5: C(5,2)=10. Choose 1 woman from 4: C(4,1)=4. Total teams = 10 x 4 = 40.
